tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

{"id":"ENG-2272","uuid":"acad23d8-0cdc-44fe-9f3d-a70ad6f443fb","title":"Show candidate nodes as results in advanced node search","description":"## Problem

* Only full discourse-node files show up as results in Advanced Node Search — an inline `#tag` line elsewhere in the vault, tagged with a configured node type, represents the same kind of node but is invisible to search.

## Solution

* Add a "Display options" menu (sliders icon) to the toolbar with a "Show candidate content" toggle.
* When on, scan the vault for lines tagged with a configured node type's `#candidate-tag` and merge them into the same ranked/filtered/sorted pipeline as regular nodes.

## Done When

* Toggling "Show candidate nodes" surfaces matching tagged lines as results.
* Node-type filtering applies to candidate nodes the same as to regular nodes.
* Opening a tag result jumps to that line.

## Out of Scope

* Scrolling to and highlighting the exact tagged line inside the preview pane — see follow-up ticket <issue id="324f4f7a-7607-4c2c-a985-591cc86abf2f" href="https://linear.app/discourse-graphs/issue/ENG-2273/scroll-to-and-highlight-the-matched-line-when-previewing-a-tagged">ENG-2273</issue>.

# Prototype

A prototype is **throwaway code that answers a question**. The question decides the shape.

## Pick a branch

Identify which question is being answered, using the user's prompt, the surrounding code, or by asking if the user is around:

- **"Does this logic / state model feel right?"** → [LOGIC.md](LOGIC.md). Build a single shareable HTML file (free-play buttons plus tabbed guided walkthroughs) that pushes the state machine through cases that are hard to reason about on paper, and that a non-developer can drive.
- **"What should this look like?"** → [UI.md](UI.md). Generate several radically different UI variations on a single route, switchable via a URL search param and a floating bottom bar.

The two branches produce very different artifacts, so getting this wrong wastes the whole prototype. If the question is genuinely ambiguous and the user isn't reachable, default to whichever branch better matches the surrounding code (a backend module → logic; a page or component → UI) and state the assumption at the top of the prototype.

## Rules that apply to both

1. **Throwaway from day one, and clearly marked as such.** Locate the prototype code close to where it will actually be used (next to the module or page it's prototyping for) so context is obvious, but name it so a casual reader can see it's a prototype, not production. For throwaway UI routes, obey whatever routing convention the project already uses; don't invent a new top-level structure.

# UI Prototype

Generate **several radically different UI variations** on a single route, switchable from a floating bottom bar. The user flips between variants in the browser, picks one (or steals bits from each), then throws the rest away.

If the question is about logic/state rather than what something looks like, this is the wrong branch. Use [LOGIC.md](LOGIC.md).

## When this is the right shape

- "What should this page look like?"
- "I want to see a few options for this dashboard before committing."
- "Try a different layout for the settings screen."
- Any time the user would otherwise spend a day picking between three vague mockups in their head.

## Two sub-shapes: strongly prefer sub-shape A

A UI prototype is much easier to judge when it's **butting up against the rest of the app**: real header, real sidebar, real data, real density. A throwaway route on its own is a vacuum: every variant looks fine in isolation. Default to sub-shape A whenever there's a plausible existing page to host the variants. Only reach for sub-shape B if the prototype genuinely has no nearby home.

### Sub-shape A: adjustment to an existing page (preferred)

The route already exists. Variants are rendered **on the same route**, gated by a `?variant=` URL search param. The existing data fetching, params, and auth all stay. Only the rendering swaps. This is the default; pick it unless there's a specific reason not to.

If the prototype is for something that doesn't yet have a page but *would naturally live inside one* (a new section of the dashboard, a new card on the settings screen, a new step in an existing flow), it's still sub-shape A. Mount the variants inside the host page.

### Sub-shape B: a new page (last resort)

Only use this when the thing being prototyped genuinely has no existing page to live inside (e.g. an entirely new top-level surface, or a flow that can't be embedded anywhere sensible).

Create a **throwaway route** following whatever routing convention the project already uses. Don't invent a new top-level structure. Name it so it's obviously a prototype (e.g. include the word `prototype` in the path or filename). Same `?variant=` pattern.

Before committing to sub-shape B, sanity-check: is there really no existing page this could be embedded in? An empty route hides design problems that a populated one would expose.

In both sub-shapes the floating bottom bar is identical.

## Process

### 1. State the question and pick N

Default to **3 variants**. More than 5 stops being radically different and starts being noise, so cap there.

Write down the plan in one line, in the prototype's location or a top-of-file comment:

> "Three variants of the settings page, switchable via `?variant=`, on the existing `/settings` route."

This works whether the user is here to push back or not.

### 2. Generate radically different variants

Draft each variant. Hold each one to:

- The page's purpose and the data it has access to.
- The project's component library / styling system (TailwindCSS, shadcn, MUI, plain CSS, whatever).
- A clear exported component name, e.g. `VariantA`, `VariantB`, `VariantC`.

Variants must be **structurally different**: different layout, different information hierarchy, different primary affordance, not just different colours. Three slightly-tweaked card grids isn't a UI prototype, it's wallpaper. If two drafts come out too similar, redo one with explicit "do not use a card grid" guidance.

### 3. Wire them together

Create a single switcher component on the route:

```tsx
// pseudo-code, adapt to the project's framework
const variant = searchParams.get('variant') ?? 'A';
return (
  <>
    {variant === 'A' && <VariantA {...data} />}
    {variant === 'B' && <VariantB {...data} />}
    {variant === 'C' && <VariantC {...data} />}
    <PrototypeSwitcher variants={['A','B','C']} current={variant} />
  </>
);
```

For sub-shape A (existing page): keep all the existing data fetching above the switcher; only the rendered subtree changes per variant.

For sub-shape B (new page): the throwaway route under `/prototype/<name>` mounts the same switcher.

### 4. Build the floating switcher

A small fixed-position bar at the bottom-centre of the screen with three pieces:

- **Left arrow**: cycles to the previous variant (wraps around).
- **Variant label**: shows the current variant key and, if the variant exports a name, that name too. e.g. `B (Sidebar layout)`.
- **Right arrow**: cycles forward (wraps around).

Behaviour:

- Clicking an arrow updates the URL search param (use the framework's router, e.g. `router.replace` on Next, `navigate` on React Router, etc) so the variant is shareable and reload-stable.
- Keyboard: `←` and `→` arrow keys also cycle. Don't intercept arrow keys when an `<input>`, `<textarea>`, or `[contenteditable]` is focused.
- Visually distinct from the page (e.g. high-contrast pill, subtle shadow) so it's obviously not part of the design being evaluated.
- Hidden in production builds: gate on `process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production'` or an equivalent check, so a stray prototype merge can't ship the bar to users.

Put the switcher in a single shared component so both sub-shapes can reuse it. Locate it wherever shared UI lives in the project.

### 5. Hand it over

Surface the URL (and the `?variant=` keys). The user will flip through whenever they get to it. The interesting feedback is usually **"I want the header from B with the sidebar from C"**, which is the actual design they want.

### 6. Capture the answer and clean up

Once a variant has won, capture the answer (which variant and why), then capture the prototype the way the [SKILL](SKILL.md) describes. Fold the winner into the real code and move the rest onto the throwaway branch, not into main:

- **Sub-shape A**: fold the winner into the existing page; drop the losing variants and the switcher from main.
- **Sub-shape B**: promote the winning variant to a real route; drop the throwaway route and the switcher from main.

The full set of variants is the primary source, so it lands on the throwaway branch, not the bin, since variant components and the switcher left in the main branch rot fast and confuse the next reader.

## Anti-patterns

- **Variants that differ only in colour or copy.** That's a tweak, not a prototype. Real variants disagree about structure.
- **Sharing too much code between variants.** A shared `<Header>` is fine; a shared `<Layout>` defeats the point. Each variant should be free to throw out the layout.
- **Wiring variants to real mutations.** Read-only prototypes are fine. If a variant needs to mutate, point it at a stub: the question is "what should this look like", not "does the backend work".
- **Promoting the prototype directly to production.** The variant code was written under prototype constraints (no tests, minimal error handling). Rewrite it properly when you fold it in.

It is stacked on other unmerged ENG-2181/2263/2264 work, so `main...head` shows 11 files.

**1. Sorting and ranking**
- **Merge:** `NodeSearchModal.tsx:457-466` appends tag candidates after the node candidates (`[...candidateState.candidates, ...tagCandidates]`) and passes the combined list to the existing `rankDiscourseNodesByTitle`. There is no special weighting, no section and no interleaving logic.
- **Scoring:** Obsidian's `prepareFuzzySearch` runs against `title`. For a candidate, the title is the cleaned-up line text. Nodes and candidates share one score scale.
- **Ties:** the sort is stable, so on equal scores nodes come before candidates.
- **Empty query:** everything is sorted by `title.localeCompare` with score 0, so candidates mix alphabetically with nodes.
- **Sort options** (`sortSearchResults`, unchanged):
  - Relevance uses the fuzzy score.
  - Title uses the cleaned-up line text.
  - Date created and Date modified use the containing file's `ctime`/`mtime`, so every line from one file ties.
  - Author uses the file's author.
- **Truncation:** sorting happens before the `MAX_VISIBLE_RESULTS = 50` cut, so candidates can push nodes out of the top 50.

**2. Scanning** (`QueryEngine.ts` `getDiscourseTagCandidates`, diff 444-496)
- **Tag mapping:** a map from `nodeType.tag.toLowerCase()` to the node type.
- **Finding lines:** it loops over `vault.getMarkdownFiles()` and reads `metadataCache.getFileCache(file).tags`, using `position.start.line` to locate each tag. Results are deduped by `(line, nodeTypeId)`. Only files with a match are read, via `cachedRead`, and a read failure skips that file.
- **When:** once, on the first toggle-on (`NodeSearchModal.tsx` diff 214-248). The result is cached in component state for the modal's lifetime and is not refreshed on keystrokes. If the toggle goes off mid-scan, the guard resets so the next toggle-on scans again.
- **Performance:** a single pass over the metadata cache (cheap), plus one read per file that has a match, awaited one at a time. There is no chunking or yielding.
- **Title:** `sanitizeTagLine` (diff 411-430) strips list, blockquote and heading markers, wikilinks, markdown links, bold/italic and code, then removes **every** `#\S+` and collapses whitespace. Lines that end up empty are dropped.
- **Subtitle:** `file.basename` in muted, smaller text (diff 181-185).

**3. Rendering**
- **Row container:** the row container's classes are unchanged, so candidate and regular rows have no margin, padding or indent difference.
- **Title wrapper:** every row, candidate or not, now wraps the title in `<div className="min-w-0 flex-1">`.
- **Candidate markers:** the subtitle line, and a badge showing the full configured tag instead of the usual 3-character badge (diff 283-287). There is no icon, label or section header.
- **Display options menu:** new `NodeDisplayOptionsMenu.tsx`, a `SearchDropdown` with a `sliders-horizontal` icon. `isActive` is set when the toggle is on. It holds one `ToggleRow` built from Obsidian's `checkbox-container mod-small`, with `role="switch"`, a mousedown `preventDefault` so the panel doesn't close, and Enter support. `SearchDropdownId` gains `"display-options"`. The toggle state is not persisted.

**4. Opening**
- `openActiveResult` passes `tagLine.lineNumber` along (diff 311-314).
- `openFileInNewTab` and `openFileInNewLeaf` accept an optional `line` and call `leaf.openFile(file, { eState: { line } })` (`openFileUtils.ts`).
- The in-modal preview does not jump to the line. That is deferred to ENG-2273, and the preview `resetKey` is still `file.path`.

**5. Filters:** yes. `filterCandidatesByNodeTypeIds` runs on the combined list, so candidates are filtered by `nodeTypeId`. An empty selection shows all types.

**6. Review comments**
- Devin raised three issues: cancelled scans never restart, one unreadable file aborts the whole scan, and a repeated tag creates duplicate rows. Commit c044bea97 addresses all three in code, but the threads are unresolved.
- Graphite's one open issue is real: cached candidates go stale if `plugin.settings.nodeTypes` changes after a successful scan, because the ref blocks a rescan.
- The PR is a draft with scope-check and full-review boxes unchecked and the Loom pending.

**7. Questionable or buggy**
- The doc comment says candidates come from "a file that isn't itself that node", but nothing excludes them. A node file containing its own tag produces both a node row and a candidate row.
- `sanitizeTagLine` has several problems:
  - `#\S+` also strips non-node tags and URL fragments like `/page#anchor`.
  - The `_` italic regex mangles `snake_case`: `foo_bar_baz` becomes `foobarbaz`.
  - The sanitize comment points to `scrollToAndFlashLine`, which doesn't exist yet (it belongs to ENG-2273).
- `console.error` in `QueryEngine` breaks the "no console in apps/obsidian" rule; a `Notice` is the expected pattern.
- Files are read one at a time with no progress indicator, which could stall on large vaults.
- Date and author sorts are meaningless within a single file, since all its lines share one value.
- The `ToggleRow` doc comments run far past the 1–2 line comment rule, and several other comment blocks do too.</result>

# Plan: ENG-2272 Show candidate nodes

## What the research found
- **Sorting in John's PR:** tagged lines are added to the end of the node list and fuzzy-scored on the same title scale as real nodes. There's no MiniSearch or semantic search anywhere; main uses Obsidian's `prepareFuzzySearch`. On equal scores nodes win, but a candidate that scores higher outranks a real node, and candidates can push real nodes out of the 50-row cap. With an empty query, both kinds are mixed together A to Z.
- **Messy left edge:** the row padding is the same for both. The problem is the badge: candidates show the full tag (`pain-points`), real nodes show 3 letters (`OBS`), so each title starts wherever its badge ends.
- **Other problems I won't carry over:**
  - A node file that contains its own tag shows up twice.
  - The title clean-up removes non-node tags and URL fragments, and turns `snake_case` into `snakecase`.
  - The scan result goes stale if you change node types.
  - It uses `console.error`, which apps/obsidian doesn't allow.
- **On main:** node types already have a `tag` field, with defaults like `clm-candidate`, but nothing scans the vault for tagged lines. `tagNodeHandler.ts` already has a `titleFromTaggedLine` helper that isn't exported; I can reuse it.

## Step 1: Prototype on a throwaway branch
I'll build three variants inside the real search modal, with a small bar at the bottom to switch between them. All three share two fixes:
- **Fixed-width badge column**, so every title starts at the same x.
- **Same badge for candidates:** a candidate gets its node type's normal 3-letter badge, outlined instead of filled.

```
A · Sections                 B · One ranked list            C · Tabs, grouped by file
┌──────────────────────────┐ ┌───────────────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────────────┐
│ NODES · 8                │ │ (OBS) Funny bugs          │  │ [All] Nodes 8 Cand. 5    │
│ (OBS) Funny bugs         │ │ [PAI] monkeys eat my ban… │  │ ▾ Obsidian LLM Plugin    │
│ (CLM) The sky is blue    │ │       monkeys.md · L12    │  │   [PAI] cant have mcp…   │
│ CANDIDATES · 5           │ │ (CLM) The sky is blue     │  │   [PAI] embeddings keep… │
│ [PAI] monkeys eat my ban…│ │ [PAI] cant have mcp serv… │  │ ▾ monkeys                │
│       monkeys.md         │ │       Obsidian LLM Plugin │  │   [PAI] monkeys eat my…  │
└──────────────────────────┘ └───────────────────────────┘  └──────────────────────────┘
 Nodes always come first;     Score alone decides order;     Each tab has its own list;
 each section ranked alone.   outline badge + source mark    "All" matches A. Candidates
                              candidates.                    sit under their source file.
```
(`( )` = filled badge for a node, `[ ]` = outlined badge for a candidate)

- **Real data:** each variant uses the real scan of tags already indexed by Obsidian (cheap), with duplicates and node files that contain their own tag excluded. That scanner is needed in the final version anyway.
- **Switching variants:** the search box is editable text, so plain ←/→ can't switch variants. The bar uses buttons plus Alt+←/→.

## Step 2: Verify the prototype and send it to you
I'll build into a test vault with `dg-obsidian-cdp-verify`, take a screenshot of each variant on a vault that has both nodes and candidates, and send them to you. You pick a variant, or mix parts of them.

## Step 3: Implement the winner on this branch
- **Toolbar:** a "Display options" menu with a sliders icon, next to the sort menu and built the same way, containing a "Show candidate nodes" toggle. It starts off each time the modal opens and isn't saved between sessions.
- **Scanner:** read Obsidian's tag index once, then rescan when node types change. Tags that aren't node tags stay in the title.
- **Filters:** node-type filtering applies to candidates.
- **Sort:** the sort rules follow the chosen variant, and the 50-row cap applies to each section separately so candidates can't push nodes out.
- **Opening a result:** jumps to the tagged line via `eState: { line }`. Highlighting the line in the preview is left to ENG-2273.
- **Prototype capture:** I'll leave a pointer to the prototype branch and your verdict on the ticket.

## Step 4: Final verification
- Unit tests for the scanner and the ranking/merge rules.
- A CDP run covering the three Done When items: the toggle surfaces tagged lines, the type filter applies to them, and Enter opens at the right line.
- `ci:validate`, then `dg-pr-adherence-check`.

**Two questions before I build:**
1. Are these three variants worth building, or should I drop or swap one? The ASCII sketches may already be enough to choose.
2. Should the toggle state be saved between modal opens? The ticket doesn't say, so I'd leave it unsaved.

content.text:
## Option B: one ranked list
Every row will have the same layout:
- **Badge column:** fixed width and left-aligned. Every badge is the node type's 3-letter code, filled for a real node and outlined for a candidate.
- **Title column:** starts at the same x on every row, and the candidate's source line sits in that same column. Nothing shifts.

```
(OBS) Funny bugs
[PAI] monkeys eat my bananas
      monkeys · L12
(CLM) The sky is blue
```

## Querying candidates without scanning the vault
Neither API offers a direct "which lines have this tag" lookup, but both give us something close.

**Obsidian:**
- There's no public way to ask "which files have `#x`". The core Search view's `tag:` query isn't exposed to plugins.
- `metadataCache.getFileCache(file).tags` gives each tag with its line and position, from Obsidian's own index in memory. Looping over it touches no disk, so it takes milliseconds even on large vaults.
- John's slow part wasn't the tag lookup. It was reading every matching file one at a time to get the line text.
- `metadataCache.getTags()` exists but is undocumented and returns only counts, not locations.

**Datacore:**
- It indexes content below the file level and has a query language with tag filters. Something like `(@list-item or @block) and #pain-points` should return the matching blocks with their line positions. List items appear to include their text, which would mean no file read for bulleted candidates.
- The plugin already uses this pattern for nodes: Datacore when it's installed, the Obsidian cache otherwise (`getFilesWithNodeTypeId`).

**Recommendation:** use the same pattern for candidates.
1. When Datacore is installed, one tag query per node-type tag.
2. Otherwise, loop over Obsidian's cached tags, then read the text only for files with a match, all at once rather than one after another. `cachedRead` is served from memory for recently opened files.

**Not yet verified:** how Datacore handles tags. I'm unsure whether `#tag` on a block also matches when the tag sits on a parent or child block, and whether paragraph blocks (not list items) carry their text. I'll test this in the running Obsidian before building on it. If Datacore gets it wrong, the Obsidian cache approach alone is fine performance-wise.

**Next:** that test first, then implement option B on this branch. Shall I go ahead?

Instead a candidate uses its node type's badge, the same 3-letter code a real node gets (`CLM` for a `clm-candidate` line), outlined instead of filled. The full tag moves to the second line. ```
(CLM) The sky is blue
[CLM] Lines of evidence suggest sky colour varies
      #clm-candidate · monkeys · L12
```

**Fallback scan:** one pass over the files, not one pass per node type.
1. Build a map from each tag to its node type once, before the loop.
2. For each file, look up each cached tag in that map. The cost depends on the number of files and tags, not on how many node types there are.
3. Record matching candidates during that same pass.
4. Read the line text only for files with a match, all at once rather than one after another.

The Datacore path gets the same treatment: one query covering all the candidate tags (`#a or #b or …`), not one query per type.

I'll collect the candidates once per modal open and rank them against each query, the same way nodes work. Sorting during the scan would buy nothing, because every keystroke re-ranks the list.

Next I'm testing Datacore's tag behaviour in the running Obsidian.

description: "How to drive the running Obsidian app programmatically over CDP to verify plugin changes, and where the fuller Playwright harness lives"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: reference
  originSessionId: 01fc3963-d706-437b-b51d-c4c4cfa1c803

**Use the personal skill `~/.claude/skills/dg-obsidian-cdp-verify` (`scripts/run.mjs`) instead of hand-writing a driver.** Most gotchas below are now handled in its code. Keep this note as the background for why.

Obsidian is Electron, so it can be driven over the Chrome DevTools Protocol. Relaunch with
`open -na /Applications/Obsidian.app --args --remote-debugging-port=9222`, then attach over
`ws` to the target from `http://127.0.0.1:9222/json/list`. Verified working August 2026 on
Obsidian 1.8.4 / macOS — 23/23 assertions driving the ENG-2113 search footer.

Key points learned the hard way:

- **Attach to an already-open vault** instead of rewriting `~/Library/Application Support/obsidian/obsidian.json`
  to select one. The rewrite is how PR #959 selects a vault and it is also that PR's worst bug —
  if launch throws afterwards, teardown never runs and the user's global Obsidian config stays clobbered.
- Several CDP page targets exist (devtools, popouts, one per vault). Pick by
  `document.querySelector(".workspace")` **and** `app.vault.getName() === "<vault>"` — title matching alone
  is not enough when multiple vaults are open.
- Reload the plugin between runs so fresh code is tested:
  `app.plugins.disablePlugin(id).then(() => app.plugins.enablePlugin(id))`. Plugin id is
  `@discourse-graph/obsidian`, so command ids look like `@discourse-graph/obsidian:open-node-search`.
- `Runtime.evaluate` bodies are wrapped in a plain function, so `await` at the top level throws —
  return a promise chain instead.
- Playwright is **not** required; ~40 lines of raw CDP over `ws` covers evaluate, `Input.dispatchKeyEvent`,
  `Input.dispatchMouseEvent`, and `Page.captureScreenshot`.
- To distinguish "new tab" from "split", compare a root-leaf count against
  `app.workspace.rootSplit.children.length` — a new tab raises leaves only, a split raises both.
  **`iterateRootLeaves` stops early when the callback returns a truthy value**, so
  `iterateRootLeaves(() => n++)` silently caps the count at 2 (post-increment returns 1 on the
  second call). Use a block body: `iterateRootLeaves(() => { n++; })`.
- **Poll conditions, never sleep.** A 10-line `waitFor(expr)` that evaluates every 25ms took one
  scenario from 24.3s to 1.2s — 8.8s of that was literal `sleep()` calls, and only 0.35s of real
  waiting was ever needed. Naive fixed-sleep CDP is slower than Playwright; polled CDP is a wash.
- Reset workspace state at the start of a scenario, or assertions inherit leftover tabs and splits.
  `getLeaf("tab")` **reuses an empty active leaf** rather than adding one, so with a dirty workspace
  a correct new-tab implementation reads as a failure.
- Close a stray modal with an Escape key event rather than a programmatic `body.click()` — a
  synthetic click on `body` does not hit the modal's background element, so it will not dismiss it.
- **The developer is using the app while the harness drives it.** A human opening tabs or modals
  mid-run perturbs state and produces failures that look like code bugs. Re-run before believing a
  causal story built on one observation: this session produced a confident, wrong diagnosis
  ("`detachLeavesOfType` + `openFile` in one `evaluate` loses the file") that failed to reproduce
  3/3 times once tested deliberately. The real cause was concurrent human interaction. A baseline
  reset at scenario start makes runs robust to this; a dedicated vault would isolate it properly.
- **Force the renderer active over CDP instead of fighting for window focus.** Two calls at connect
  time make occlusion throttling irrelevant:
  `Page.setWebLifecycleState {state:"active"}` and `Emulation.setFocusEmulationEnabled {enabled:true}`.
  Without them, `osascript -e 'tell application "Obsidian" to activate'` only holds until the next
  command returns focus to the terminal, and Reading view silently renders an **empty**
  `.markdown-preview-section` — links, Properties and backlinks all absent, no error. Verified
  September 2026 on Obsidian 1.13.7: the identical scenario went from `body link rendered: false`
  to `true` with those two calls added. The note below still describes the underlying throttling.
- **The Obsidian window must be visible (`document.visibilityState === "visible"`) while scenarios
  run.** When it is covered/minimised/on another Space, Chromium throttles the renderer's timers —
  100 ms → 300–900 ms, and after ~5 min hidden to once per minute — so anything built on
  `setTimeout` (a 500 ms save debounce, a sync debounce, a poll loop *inside* the page) silently
  stalls. It presents as "the feature is broken" (writes land minutes later) with zero errors.
  ENG-2107 lost an hour to this. Check `visibilityState` and a 100 ms timer's real latency before
  believing a timing failure; `electronWindow.setAlwaysOnTop(true)` helps only until focus changes,
  so ask the user to click the window and poll `visibilityState` before firing the scenario.
- The auto-mode classifier blocks quit-and-relaunch as one compound Bash command; run the steps separately.
- **`editor.hasFocus()` is not measurable from CDP.** It reads `false` even for a plain
  `editor.focus()` with no modal involved and `document.hasFocus() === true`; no element holds DOM
  focus at all (`document.activeElement` is the top-level app div). Take a **baseline** measurement
  of the same assertion outside the feature under test before believing a focus failure — ENG-2114
  looked like a focus regression until the baseline failed identically. Assert the observable
  consequence instead (cursor position advanced past the inserted text).
- **Stale `.modal-container` elements poison selectors.** A scenario that times out or throws leaves
  its modal in the DOM, so the next run's `querySelector(".modal-container .modal")` reads the *old*
  modal — producing "footer missing the action" and "modal did not close" failures while the feature
  actually works. Start every scenario with
  `document.querySelectorAll(".modal-container").forEach(el => el.remove())`.
- The plugin **folder** is `discourse-graphs` but the **id** is `@discourse-graph/obsidian`; passing the
  folder name to `disablePlugin`/`enablePlugin` silently no-ops (`loaded: false`, `manifests[folder]`
  undefined). Read the real id from `app.plugins.manifests`, whose `dir` field maps id → folder.

- `detachLeavesOfType("markdown")` followed by `getLeaf(true)` throws **"No tab group found."** —
  detaching the last markdown leaf destroys the tab group the new leaf would go in. Reuse
  `getMostRecentLeaf()` instead of clearing first.
- Obsidian's **Properties** block and the **backlinks-in-document** panel contain **no
  `a.internal-link` anchors**: a link property renders as `div.multi-select-pill-content.internal-link`
  and backlink entries carry no anchors at all. A markdown post processor that queries
  `a.internal-link` therefore cannot leak into either, whatever it scans. Both panels are also
  collapsed/`display:none` by default, so a scenario must expand Properties
  (`.metadata-properties-heading`) and run `backlink:toggle-backlinks-in-document` before asserting.
- **A markdown post processor receives its element DETACHED (`el.isConnected === false`) during a
  normal Reading view render**, but attached and inside `.modal-container` when the plugin calls
  `MarkdownRenderer.render` itself. So `el.closest(".markdown-reading-view")` is null on the real
  path and is the wrong guard; `el.closest(".modal-container")` is the correct tell for "this is our
  own modal preview". Measured with a throwaway `registerMarkdownPostProcessor` probe pushing to a
  `window.__probe` array — a cheap pattern for any question about post processor call context.
- zsh expands `${VAR}` inside `node -e "..."`, silently turning `plugins['${ID}']` into `plugins['']`.
  Write the scenario to a `.mjs` file instead of passing it through `-e`.

A fuller Playwright + CDP harness already exists on branch
`worktree-eng-1583-automate-obsidian-dev-environment-load-and-visual-validation` (PR #959, ENG-1583):
launch, vault switching, command palette driving, modal helpers, step screenshots. It is open with
CHANGES_REQUESTED — the blocking objection is documentation quality, not the mechanism — and is far
behind main. Reuse its `e2e/helpers/obsidian-setup.ts` rather than rediscovering the launch tricks.

Unrelated dev-loop gotcha hit while doing this: editing only a file under `apps/obsidian/src/styles/`
never triggers a rebuild, because the concatenation runs in esbuild's `onEnd` while those files sit
outside its module graph. Touch a `.ts` file to force it. See [[feedback-obsidian-no-console]] for the
related Notice-instead-of-console rule in this app.

---
name: dg-obsidian-cdp-verify
description: Prove an apps/obsidian change works in the real Obsidian app by driving it over the Chrome DevTools Protocol. One command launches or attaches to Obsidian on a test vault slot, builds this worktree into it, runs scenario modules, and writes a scenario matrix plus screenshots for pr-evidence and create-pr. Use for live Obsidian verification before a PR, or when asked "does this actually work in Obsidian?".
---

# Obsidian CDP verify

## The one command

From the worktree root:

```sh
node ~/.claude/skills/dg-obsidian-cdp-verify/scripts/run.mjs \
  --slot 1 --marker "<string only this change's bundle contains>" \
  --scenario path/to/scenarios.mjs [--scenario more.mjs] [--port 9222] [--skip-build]
```

It runs doctor → launch → deliver → scenarios → cleanup and prints the `last-run.json` path, the scenario matrix, and the `pr-evidence` args. Exit codes: 0 all pass, 1 failure, 2 vault locked, 3 marker missing.

Write scenario files in the session scratchpad, not the repo.

## Launch

- Slots come from `OBSIDIAN_VERIFY_VAULTS` in `<worktree>/apps/obsidian/.env`. It takes a JSON array or a comma list of plugin dirs or vault roots. `--slot N` is 1-based and defaults to 1.
- If Obsidian is running on the debug port, the script attaches.
- If it's running without the port, the script quits Obsidian and relaunches it with `--remote-debugging-port`. Trang approved this; the windows come back.
- If it isn't running, the script launches it with the port.
- It then opens the slot vault through `obsidian://open?path=` and waits for a page target where `.workspace` exists and `app.vault.adapter.basePath` matches the vault.
- It writes the lock `<vault>/.obsidian/dg-verify.lock` (`{pid, branch, startedAt}`) and releases it in `finally`.

## Doctor

`scripts/doctor.mjs [--slot N]` is read-only and prints JSON: the resolved slot, the lock and the Obsidian state. If another live run holds the lock, it exits 2 and asks you to switch slot. A lock left by a dead pid is ignored.

## Deliver

`scripts/deliver.mjs --marker <str>` also runs on its own.

1. `OBSIDIAN_PLUGIN_PATH=<slot plugin dir> tsx scripts/build.ts` runs once in `apps/obsidian`. It also writes `apps/obsidian/dist`, which is gitignored.
2. It greps the vault's `main.js` for `--marker` and fails if the marker is absent.
3. It reloads the plugin. The plugin id and folder are resolved from the manifests.
4. It greps again.
5. It warns about competing `dev.ts`/esbuild watchers. Your own worktree's watcher counts too, if it mirrors into the same vault.

The harness also hashes `main.js` before and after the scenarios. If it changed, the run is marked invalid.

## Drive: scenario contract

A module's `export default` is one scenario or an array of them:

```js
export default {
  name: "Search modal renders",                 // matrix row + screenshot name
  input: "run open-node-search",                // matrix text
  expected: "modal with a textbox and footer",  // matrix text
  setup: async (ctx) => ({ /* state; snapshot anything you change */ }),  // optional
  run: async ({ client, json, vault }, state) => {
    await client.evaluate(`return app.commands.executeCommandById(${json(`${vault.pluginId}:open-node-search`)});`);
    await client.waitFor(`!!document.querySelector(".dg-node-search-modal [role=textbox]")`);
    return client.evaluate(`document.querySelectorAll(".dg-search-footer-action").length`);
  },
  expect: (actual, state) => ({ pass: actual > 0, actual: `${actual} footer actions` }),  // or a boolean
  teardown: async (ctx, state) => {},           // optional: restore what setup changed
};
```

- `ctx` has `client`, `vault` (`root`, `pluginId`, `pluginDir`), `branch`, `json`, `verifyPath(name)` and `writeNote(name, body)`. `writeNote` creates or overwrites `_verify/<branch>/<name>` and returns its path.
- `client` has `evaluate`, `waitFor`, `key`, `typeText`, `pressEscape`, `screenshot`, `reloadPlugin`, `clearModals` and `send` (raw CDP).
- The harness does these for you:
  - Before each scenario, it clears modals and restores the layout captured at the start of the run.
  - After `run`, it takes a screenshot.
  - A thrown error becomes a failing row.
- The worked example is `examples/insert-link-at-cursor.mjs` (ENG-2114, 3 scenarios).

## Evidence

- The artifacts go to `<worktree>/local/obsidian-cdp/artifacts/<branch>/<runStamp>/`: `<n>-<slug>.png` and `last-run.json` (`results[]` of `{scenario, input, expected, actual, pass, screenshot}`).
- Paste the printed matrix into create-pr's Evidence section.
- Upload the screenshots with pr-evidence, using the printed args:

```sh
./apps/roam/node_modules/.bin/tsx ~/.claude/skills/pr-evidence/upload.ts --harness obsidian-cdp <printed args>
```

## Cleanup

- Cleanup dismisses modals (Escape, then force-removes leftover `.modal-container`), restores the baseline layout and releases the lock.
- **It never deletes folders or notes.** `_verify/<branch>/` persists, and reruns overwrite its notes.
- Scenarios that change vault or app settings must restore them in `teardown`.

## Gotchas

These are the ones the code can't handle for you.

| Symptom | Cause / fix |
| --- | --- |
| Double-handled keypress | Pass `type` to `client.key` only through its loop. Never send your own `keyDown`. |
| `editor.hasFocus()` false while focus looks right | This can't be measured over CDP. Assert the consequence instead, e.g. the cursor moved past the inserted text. |
| File content assertion fails, editor looks right | Saves are debounced (about 2s). `waitFor` on `app.vault.read(...)`, and don't read once. |
| `getLeaf(true)` throws "No tab group found" | Every markdown leaf was detached. Use `getLeaf("tab")`. |
| Top-level `await` throws in `evaluate` | Bodies run in a plain function. Return an async IIFE or a promise chain. |
| `iterateRootLeaves` count caps at 2 | A truthy callback return stops the iteration. Use a block body `{ n++; }`. |
| Escape handler in a modal child never wins | Obsidian's modal scope runs first. Push a `Scope` with `app.keymap.pushScope`. |
| Styling CodeMirror spans disappears on focus or scroll | Use a CM6 decoration, not MutationObserver stamping. A widget's `ignoreEvent()` must stay `true` for clicks. |
| Selectors from an old ENG example don't match | The UI drifts. The node search input is now a contenteditable `[role=textbox]`, not an `<input>`. |
| Flaky failure that looks like a code bug | Trang may be using the app mid-run. Rerun before believing a single observation. |
| Timers stall, writes land minutes late | Focus emulation normally prevents this. If it recurs, check `document.visibilityState` and ask Trang to show the window. |
| zsh eats `${VAR}` in `node -e` | Write scenarios to `.mjs` files. |

doctor.mjs
driver.mjs
harness.mjs
launch.mjs
run.mjs

  --slot 1 --marker "<string only this change's bundle contains>" \
  --scenario path/to/scenarios.mjs [--scenario more.mjs] [--port 9222] [--skip-build]
```

It runs doctor → launch → deliver → scenarios → cleanup and prints the `last-run.json` path, the scenario matrix, and the `pr-evidence` args. Exit codes: 0 all pass, 1 failure, 2 vault locked, 3 marker missing.

Write scenario files in the session scratchpad, not the repo.

## Launch

- Slots come from `OBSIDIAN_VERIFY_VAULTS` in `<worktree>/apps/obsidian/.env`. It takes a JSON array or a comma list of plugin dirs or vault roots. `--slot N` is 1-based and defaults to 1.
- If Obsidian is running on the debug port, the script attaches.
- If it's running without the port, the script quits Obsidian and relaunches it with `--remote-debugging-port`. Trang approved this; the windows come back.
- If it isn't running, the script launches it with the port.
- It then opens the slot vault through `obsidian://open?path=` and waits for a page target where `.workspace` exists and `app.vault.adapter.basePath` matches the vault.
- It writes the lock `<vault>/.obsidian/dg-verify.lock` (`{pid, branch, startedAt}`) and releases it in `finally`.

## Doctor

`scripts/doctor.mjs [--slot N]` is read-only and prints JSON: the resolved slot, the lock and the Obsidian state. If another live run holds the lock, it exits 2 and asks you to switch slot. A lock left by a dead pid is ignored.

## Deliver

`scripts/deliver.mjs --marker <str>` also runs on its own.

1. `OBSIDIAN_PLUGIN_PATH=<slot plugin dir> tsx scripts/build.ts` runs once in `apps/obsidian`. It also writes `apps/obsidian/dist`, which is gitignored.
2. It greps the vault's `main.js` for `--marker` and fails if the marker is absent.
3. It reloads the plugin. The plugin id and folder are resolved from the manifests.
4. It greps again.
5. It warns about competing `dev.ts`/esbuild watchers. Your own worktree's watcher counts too, if it mirrors into the same vault.

The harness also hashes `main.js` before and after the scenarios. If it changed, the run is marked invalid.

## Drive: scenario contract

A module's `export default` is one scenario or an array of them:

```js
export default {
  name: "Search modal renders",                 // matrix row + screenshot name
  input: "run open-node-search",                // matrix text
  expected: "modal with a textbox and footer",  // matrix text
  setup: async (ctx) => ({ /* state; snapshot anything you change */ }),  // optional
  run: async ({ client, json, vault }, state) => {
    await client.evaluate(`return app.commands.executeCommandById(${json(`${vault.pluginId}:open-node-search`)});`);
    await client.waitFor(`!!document.querySelector(".dg-node-search-modal [role=textbox]")`);
    return client.evaluate(`document.querySelectorAll(".dg-search-footer-action").length`);
  },
  expect: (actual, state) => ({ pass: actual > 0, actual: `${actual} footer actions` }),  // or a boolean
  teardown: async (ctx, state) => {},           // optional: restore what setup changed
};
```

- `ctx` has `client`, `vault` (`root`, `pluginId`, `pluginDir`), `branch`, `json`, `verifyPath(name)` and `writeNote(name, body)`. `writeNote` creates or overwrites `_verify/<branch>/<name>` and returns its path.
- `client` has `evaluate`, `waitFor`, `key`, `typeText`, `pressEscape`, `screenshot`, `reloadPlugin`, `clearModals` and `send` (raw CDP).
- The harness does these for you:
  - Before each scenario, it clears modals and restores the layout captured at the start of the run.
  - After `run`, it takes a screenshot.
  - A thrown error becomes a failing row.
- The worked example is `examples/insert-link-at-cursor.mjs` (ENG-2114, 3 scenarios).

## Evidence

- The artifacts go to `<worktree>/local/obsidian-cdp/artifacts/<branch>/<runStamp>/`: `<n>-<slug>.png` and `last-run.json` (`results[]` of `{scenario, input, expected, actual, pass, screenshot}`).
- Paste the printed matrix into create-pr's Evidence section.
- Upload the screenshots with pr-evidence, using the printed args:

```sh
./apps/roam/node_modules/.bin/tsx ~/.claude/skills/pr-evidence/upload.ts --harness obsidian-cdp <printed args>
```

## Cleanup

- Cleanup dismisses modals (Escape, then force-removes leftover `.modal-container`), restores the baseline layout and releases the lock.
- **It never deletes folders or notes.** `_verify/<branch>/` persists, and reruns overwrite its notes.
- Scenarios that change vault or app settings must restore them in `teardown`.

## Gotchas

These are the ones the code can't handle for you.

| Symptom | Cause / fix |
| --- | --- |
| Double-handled keypress | Pass `type` to `client.key` only through its loop. Never send your own `keyDown`. |
| `editor.hasFocus()` false while focus looks right | This can't be measured over CDP. Assert the consequence instead, e.g. the cursor moved past the inserted text. |
| File content assertion fails, editor looks right | Saves are debounced (about 2s). `waitFor` on `app.vault.read(...)`, and don't read once. |
| `getLeaf(true)` throws "No tab group found" | Every markdown leaf was detached. Use `getLeaf("tab")`. |
| Top-level `await` throws in `evaluate` | Bodies run in a plain function. Return an async IIFE or a promise chain. |
| `iterateRootLeaves` count caps at 2 | A truthy callback return stops the iteration. Use a block body `{ n++; }`. |
| Escape handler in a modal child never wins | Obsidian's modal scope runs first. Push a `Scope` with `app.keymap.pushScope`. |
| Styling CodeMirror spans disappears on focus or scroll | Use a CM6 decoration, not MutationObserver stamping. A widget's `ignoreEvent()` must stay `true` for clicks. |
| Selectors from an old ENG example don't match | The UI drifts. The node search input is now a contenteditable `[role=textbox]`, not an `<input>`. |
| Flaky failure that looks like a code bug | Trang may be using the app mid-run. Rerun before believing a single observation. |
| Timers stall, writes land minutes late | Focus emulation normally prevents this. If it recurs, check `document.visibilityState` and ask Trang to show the window. |
| zsh eats `${VAR}` in `node -e` | Write scenarios to `.mjs` files. |

content.text:
I tested it in `dgDevVault`, which has Datacore 0.1.29 installed. Datacore only fully works for bulleted lines. For other line shapes it can't tell us which line holds the tag, or what that line says.

The test note had 8 tagged lines in different shapes:

| Line shape | Obsidian metadata cache | Datacore |
|---|---|---|
| List item, nested item, task | ✅ exact line | ✅ `@list-item`: exact `$line` and `$text`, no file read needed |
| Paragraph, where the tag is on its 2nd line | ✅ exact line | ⚠️ `@block` returns the whole paragraph with no text, and no way to know which of its lines holds the tag |
| Blockquote | ✅ exact line | ⚠️ same problem as paragraphs |
| Heading | ✅ exact line | ❌ only the whole `@section`, which also picks up every tag below the heading |
| Untagged parent of a tagged child | ✅ not matched | ✅ `@list-item` doesn't match it, but a `@block` list does |

The combined query (`#clm-candidate or #evd-candidate`) worked as one query.

**What this means:** with Datacore, we'd still need the metadata cache for the tag's line and a file read for every paragraph, quote or heading candidate. So the Datacore path wouldn't replace the fallback. It would run beside it and only save the read for bulleted lines. That's two code paths, and results could disagree when the two indexes are out of sync.

**My recommendation:** use one path, the single scan of the metadata cache you described, for everyone.
1. Loop over each file's cached tags and look each one up in a map from tag to node type.
2. Record every match with its line number during that pass. This covers every line shape and needs no Datacore.
3. Read only the files that had a match, all at once rather than one after another, using `cachedRead`.

The lookup runs in memory; the only disk access is reading those files.

If you still want Datacore, a hybrid would work: Datacore `@list-item` for bulleted lines, the metadata cache for everything else. In my view the extra code path isn't worth saving a few reads.

The test left `_verify/eng-2272-…/datacore-spike.md` in `dgDevVault`. The test harness never deletes notes, so remove it whenever you like.

Metadata cache only, or the hybrid?

content.text:
Here are six ways to tell candidates apart within the single ranked list. In every one, badges and titles start at the same x on every row. `●` = a filled badge in the node type's colour.

**1. Filled vs outlined badge** (what I proposed)
```
(CLM) The sky is blue
[CLM] Sky colour varies by latitude
      #clm-candidate · monkeys · L12
```
Quiet, but outlined and filled look alike at a glance when colours are pale (like your yellow INS).

**2. Icon column in front of the badge**
```
📄 (CLM) The sky is blue
#  (CLM) Sky colour varies by latitude
         monkeys · L12
```
A fixed-width Lucide icon, `file-text` for a node and `hash` for a candidate. It's clear in one glance, even in greyscale, but costs about 20px of width.

**3. Faded candidate, like Obsidian's unresolved links**
```
(CLM) The sky is blue
(CLM) Sky colour varies by latitude        ← title in muted text, badge at 50% opacity
      #clm-candidate · monkeys · L12
```
Obsidian users already read "faded = not a real note yet" from unresolved links. The catch is that candidates look less important, which is wrong when one is the best match for the query.

**4. Tag chip at the end of the row**
```
(CLM) The sky is blue
(CLM) Sky colour varies by latitude   #clm-candidate
      monkeys · L12
```
The left side is identical for every row, so scanning is easiest. The full tag appears in the tag's own style, so it looks like what the user typed. The chip takes title width, and titles truncate sooner.

**5. Accent bar on the left edge**
```
▌(CLM) The sky is blue                     ← 2px bar in the node type colour
 (CLM) Sky colour varies by latitude       ← no bar
       monkeys · L12
```
Nodes feel "solid" and candidates "loose". It's subtle, and hard to read on its own without a legend.

**6. Two-line row only for candidates**
```
(CLM) The sky is blue
  ↳ "Sky colour varies by latitude"        ← quoted line, kept together with its source
     in monkeys · L12
```
This reads as "a line inside a note", which is literally what a candidate is. It's the tallest option, so fewer results fit in the list.

**My pick: 2 + 4 combined.** The icon column carries the node/candidate difference, and the chip at the end shows the exact tag. Each is a clear signal on its own, and neither moves the badge or title. If you'd rather keep it minimal, use 3 alone. It's the most Obsidian-native, but it downplays good candidates.

Which one or combination do you want? The metadata-cache-only vs hybrid question from before is still open too.

content.text:
Filled vs outlined it is.

On Datacore, it's slightly worse than that: it doesn't return the paragraph text at all. For your example it returns one `paragraph` block with the tag attached, a block-level position, and **no `$text` field**. So we get neither line, only "somewhere in this paragraph there's a `#candidate-node-tag`". I didn't print the exact position span in the test, but it's one entry for the whole block, not per line.

To show only "change line here", we'd still have to:
1. Know which line inside the block has the tag. Datacore doesn't say; Obsidian's metadata cache does, with the exact line number.
2. Read that line from the file.

Bulleted lines are the one exception. There Datacore returns the item's own line and text, so `- change line here #candidate-node-tag` would come back as just that item.

The metadata cache gives exactly the behaviour you want for every line shape, which matches how the create-node-from-tag flow works (`titleFromTaggedLine` in `tagNodeHandler.ts`). Each candidate is the tagged line alone, stripped of list markers and the node tag:

```
line 1: blah blah blah blah
change line here #candidate-node-tag     →  candidate title: "change line here", L2
```

Here's the plan, unless you object:
- **Finding candidates:** metadata cache only, in one pass. No Datacore path.
- **Title:** built by reusing `titleFromTaggedLine`, which I'll export. It removes only the node-type tags, so other tags and URL fragments stay intact.
- **Visuals:** option B, the one ranked list, with filled vs outlined badges from a fixed-width column.

Go ahead and implement?

Base directory for this skill: /Users/trang.doan/.claude/skills/checkpoint

# Checkpoint — record session context

Persist the **reasoning layer** of this work session (goal, decisions, dead ends,
constraints, next step) to the Obsidian vault, keyed to the current worktree.
Files are plain markdown written directly — no MCP, no Obsidian required running.

## Steps

### 1. Resolve where to write
Run the helper from the current worktree:

```bash
bash ~/.claude/scripts/session-context.sh resolve
```

It prints `TICKET`, `BRANCH`, `WORKTREE`, `SESSION_DIR`, `CONTEXT_FILE`,
`LOG_FILE`, `STAMP`, `CONTEXT_EXISTS` and creates the folders. **Only write to the
`CONTEXT_FILE` and `LOG_FILE` paths it gives you** — never elsewhere in the vault.
If it errors (not a git repo / detached HEAD), tell the user and stop.

### 2. Read existing context if present
If `CONTEXT_EXISTS=yes`, read `CONTEXT_FILE` first so you UPDATE it rather than
overwrite history. Digest sections get rewritten; accreting sections get appended.

### 3. Gather the reasoning layer
Reconstruct from this session's conversation + git. If a ticket id is present and
Linear is available, you may fetch the title/URL with `mcp__linear-server__get_issue`.
Apply the **extraction rubric** below to decide what is worth recording.

### 4. Write `_context.md`
Use the template at `~/.claude/skills/checkpoint/template.md` as the structure.
- If new file: fill the template. Set `created`/`updated` to today, `sessions: 1`.
- If updating: rewrite digest sections (TL;DR, Approved plan, Current state, Next
  step, Open questions, key_files, status), **append** to accreting sections (Key
  decisions, Dead ends, Constraints, Gotchas, Interventions) with a dated bullet,
  bump `updated` to today and increment `sessions`.
- **Approved plan:** write it only when the user approves a plan (gate 1), verbatim

# Test-Driven Development

TDD is the red → green loop. This skill is the reference that makes that loop produce tests worth keeping: what a good test is, where tests go, the anti-patterns, and the rules of the loop. Every section applies on every cycle: consult them before and during the loop, not after.

When exploring the codebase, read `CONTEXT.md` (if it exists) so test names and interface vocabulary match the project's domain language, and respect ADRs in the area you're touching.

## What a good test is

Tests verify behavior through public interfaces, not implementation details. Code can change entirely; tests shouldn't. A good test reads like a specification: "user can checkout with valid cart" tells you exactly what capability exists, and it survives refactors because it doesn't care about internal structure.

See [tests.md](tests.md) for examples and [mocking.md](mocking.md) for mocking guidelines.

## Seams: where tests go

A **seam** is the public boundary you test at: the interface where you observe behavior without reaching inside. Tests live at seams, never against internals.

**Test only at pre-agreed seams.** Before writing any test, write down the seams under test and confirm them with the user. No test is written at an unconfirmed seam. You can't test everything, so agreeing the seams up front is how testing effort lands on the critical paths and complex logic instead of every edge case.

Ask: "What's the public interface, and which seams should we test?"

When the shape of that interface is itself in question (how deep the module is, where the seam belongs, what the interface should expose), call the Skill tool with "codebase-design" for the vocabulary. It is the shared source of the module, interface, depth, seam, adapter, leverage and locality terms, and it is a reference to consult, not a session to run.

## Anti-patterns

- **Implementation-coupled**: mocks internal collaborators, tests private methods, or verifies through a side channel (querying the database instead of using the interface). The tell: the test breaks when you refactor but behavior hasn't changed.
- **Tautological**: the assertion recomputes the expected value the way the code does (`expect(add(a, b)).toBe(a + b)`, a snapshot derived by hand the same way, a constant asserted equal to itself), so it passes by construction and can never disagree with the code. Expected values must come from an independent source of truth: a known-good literal, a worked example, the spec.
- **Horizontal slicing**: writing all tests first, then all implementation. Bulk tests verify _imagined_ behavior: you test the _shape_ of things rather than user-facing behavior, the tests go insensitive to real changes, and you commit to test structure before understanding the implementation. Work in **vertical slices** instead: one test → one implementation → repeat, each test a **tracer bullet** that responds to what the last cycle taught you.

## Rules of the loop

- **Red before green.** Write the failing test first, then only enough code to pass it. Don't anticipate future tests or add speculative features.
- **One slice at a time.** One seam, one test, one minimal implementation per cycle.
- **Refactoring is not part of the loop.** It belongs to the review stage (see the `code-review` skill), not the red → green implementation cycle.

Before writing any tests, the TDD skill needs us to agree where they go. I propose three places to test. Each is a public function, and the tests would check what it returns, not how it gets there.

**1. Collecting candidates:** `QueryEngine.getCandidateNodes(nodeTypes)`, a new function. Tests run against a fake app that supplies files, cached tags and file contents. It should:
- return one candidate per tagged line, with that line's number, node type and tag. This covers paragraphs (including a tag on a paragraph's 2nd line), list items, tasks, headings and quotes.
- use only that line as the title, cleaned up by `titleFromTaggedLine`.
- match tags case-insensitively, and ignore tags that don't belong to any node type.
- skip a node file's own tag, so a node that contains its own tag doesn't show up twice.
- return a line tagged with two node types as two candidates, one per type.
- drop lines whose title is empty once cleaned up, e.g. a line containing only the tag.
- skip a file it can't read, without failing the rest.
- read only the files that had a match.

**2. Ranking nodes and candidates together:** the existing `rankDiscourseNodesByTitle`, now given both nodes and candidates. It should:
- filter candidates by node type exactly like nodes.
- put nodes and candidates on one score scale, so a better-matching candidate outranks a weaker node.
- put nodes before candidates on equal scores.

**3. UI behaviour:** checked in the real Obsidian over CDP, not unit tests. That covers the toggle, row alignment (measuring each title's left x), filled vs outlined badges, and Enter opening the tagged line.

I'm leaving `sortSearchResults` and the menu component out of unit tests because they barely change.

Are these the right places to test? Once you confirm, I'll start the first red → green cycle on collecting candidates.

You are an expert senior software engineer specializing in modern web development, with deep expertise in TypeScript, React, Next.js (App Router), and Tailwind CSS. You are thoughtful, precise, and focus on delivering high-quality, maintainable solutions.

This repository uses Turborepo.

## Apps & Packages

`apps`

- apps/website: The public-facing website for Discourse Graphs, Uses Next.js.
- apps/roam: The Roam Research extension that implements the Discourse Graph protocol.
- apps/obsidian: The Obsidian plugin that implements the Discourse Graph protocol.

`packages`

- packages/tailwind-config: Shared tailwind config
- packages/typescript-config: Shared tsconfig.jsons
- packages/eslint-config: ESLint preset
- packages/ui: Core React components

## Git & Publishing Conventions

### Agent-created Engineering tickets

For all agent-created Engineering tickets, including direct Linear tool calls and tickets created through other skills, use [dg-create-engineering-ticket](.agents/skills/dg-create-engineering-ticket/SKILL.md). Create them in `Ticket Draft` with exactly one workspace provenance label from the `Created by` group: `Created by Claude`, `Created by Codex`, or `Created by LLM` for another or unknown agent. Record the creation skills actually used in `Notes`, and verify those fields after creation. If no skill was used, record `Created with: direct agent workflow (no skill)` and still apply the same review rules.

The requesting human reviews intent, scope, acceptance criteria, and ticket-writing standards before approving a move to `Triage` or `Backlog`. Keep the provenance label after approval. See the skill for transitions and missing-configuration handling. This applies to new tickets; do not retrospectively classify existing tickets.

### Branch Naming

When working on Linear issues, prefer using the Linear-provided branch name when available. Linear automatically generates branch names in the format `eng-####-descriptive-name` (e.g., `eng-1912-scaffold-repocontent-model`).

- Use Linear's generated branch name for consistency and traceability
- Branch names should be lowercase with hyphens separating words
- Include the Linear ticket ID at the start of the branch name

### Pull Request Titles

PR titles for Linear-backed work should follow this format:

- Format: `ENG-#### Ticket title`
- The ticket ID must be uppercased (e.g., `ENG-1912` not `eng-1912`)
- Follow the ticket ID with the exact Linear ticket title
- Example: `ENG-1912 Scaffold @repo/content-model`

### Pull Request Bodies

When creating or updating a pull request body:

- Start with `.github/pull_request_template.md`. Preserve its headings and guidance instead of adding substitute sections.
- Treat the Linear ticket as the source of truth. Do not restate it in the pull request body.
- Do not add a file-by-file summary, implementation diary, investigation log, full command output, or unrelated pre-existing issues. For PRs over 400 changed lines, excluding tests, include a concise split justification, main review entry points, and testing path in Reviewer brief.
- Put line-specific implementation context in inline GitHub comments.
- Put any non-obvious rules that future changes must preserve in code comments, tests, or documentation, not only in the pull request.
- Remove empty optional sections and anything that does not help review the diff.

## Required standards

- Read and follow [STYLE_GUIDE.md](STYLE_GUIDE.md) and the nested `AGENTS.md` files that apply to changed files before editing or reviewing code.
- Follow [PR_GUIDELINES.md](PR_GUIDELINES.md) for scope, verification, and review requirements. General code standards live in the style guide; app-specific instructions remain in nested `AGENTS.md` files.
- Before handoff or requesting review, run `$dg-pr-adherence-check` from `.agents/skills/dg-pr-adherence-check/SKILL.md` against the final diff and available PR metadata. Resolve findings or report them explicitly, including missing evidence. Rerun affected checks after changes.

content.content: @AGENTS.md

You are working on the Obsidian plugin that implements the Discourse Graph protocol.

## Dependencies

Prefer existing dependencies from package.json.

## Obsidian Style Guide

Use the obsidian style guide from help.obsidian.md/style-guide and docs.obsidian.md/Developer+policies.

### Icons

Platform-native UI.
Lucide and custom Obsidian icons can be used alongside detailed elements to provide a visual representation of a feature.

Example: In the ribbon on the left, select Create new canvas ( lucide-layout-dashboard.svg > icon ) to create a canvas in the same folder as the active file.

Guidelines for icons

Store icons in the Attachments/icons folder.
Add the prefix lucide- before the Lucide icon name.
Add the prefix obsidian-icon- before the Obsidian icon name.
Example: The icon for creating a new canvas should be named lucide-layout-dashboard.

Use the SVG version of the icons available.
Icons should be 18 pixels in width, 18 pixels in height, and have a stroke width of 1.5. You can adjust these settings in the SVG data.
Adjusting size and stroke in an SVG.
Utilize the icon anchor in embedded images, to tweak the spacing around the icon so that it aligns neatly with the text in the vicinity.
Icons should be surrounded by parenthesis. ( lucide-cog.svg > icon )
Example: ( ![[lucide-cog.svg#icon]] )

### Function guides

- Any function that deals with querying vault's frontmatter, default to using Datacore API first, then write fallback where you use `plugin.app.vault.getMarkdownFiles()` to iterate through each file's frontmatter

## Plugin Store Guidelines

These rules must be followed for the plugin to be accepted into the Obsidian community plugin store.

### Security

- Never use `innerHTML`, `outerHTML`, or `insertAdjacentHTML` with user-controlled content
- Use Obsidian DOM helpers instead: `createEl()`, `createDiv()`, `createSpan()`

### App instance

- Always use `this.app` — never the global `app` object

### Event listeners

- Register all event listeners via `this.registerEvent()` so they are automatically cleaned up on plugin unload

### UI text

- Use sentence case in settings headings and labels (not title case)
- Prefer `setHeading()` over raw HTML heading elements (`<h1>`, `<h2>`, etc.)

### Commands

- Do not set default hotkeys — they conflict with other plugins
- Use the correct callback type: `callback` for always-available commands, `checkCallback` when the command is conditionally available, or the editor variants for editor-scoped commands
- Do not manually prepend the plugin ID to command IDs — Obsidian adds it automatically

### Workspace

- Do not store references to custom views — look them up fresh each time they are needed
  Don't do this:
  `this.registerView(MY_VIEW_TYPE, () => this.view = new MyCustomView());`
  Do this instead:
  `this.registerView(MY_VIEW_TYPE, () => new MyCustomView());`
  To access the view from your plugin, use `Workspace.getActiveLeavesOfType():`

```
for (let leaf of app.workspace.getActiveLeavesOfType(MY_VIEW_TYPE)) {
  let view = leaf.view;
  if (view instanceof MyCustomView) {
    // ...
  }
